paragraphs.heading: Order does not matter
paragraphs.text: An abelian group, also known as a commutative group, is a group where combining two elements gives the same answer whichever one you write first. Put another way, its operation is commutative. A group whose operation fails this test is called non-abelian, or non-commutative. Camille Jordan chose the name to honour Niels Henrik Abel, a mathematician from Norway, who had found that when the group of a polynomial is commutative, the roots of that polynomial can be calculated using radicals.

paragraphs.heading: The other rules
paragraphs.text: Commutativity sits on top of the usual group rules. Grouping does not matter, so (a⋅b)⋅c always equals a⋅(b⋅c). There is an identity element e that leaves everything alone: e⋅a = a⋅e = a. And each element a has a partner b that brings it back to the identity, with a⋅b = b⋅a = e.

paragraphs.heading: Familiar examples
paragraphs.text: The integers under addition are the model case. Adding two integers gives another integer, addition is associative, zero is the identity, each n has the inverse −n, and n + m = m + n. The real numbers under addition form one too, and so do the nonzero reals under multiplication. Every cyclic group is abelian, which covers the integers modulo n, written ℤ/nℤ. Even the group holding nothing but its identity element counts.

paragraphs.heading: Where it fails
paragraphs.text: Matrices show how the rule can break. Multiplying two matrices usually gives a different result in the other order, so matrices, even invertible ones, generally fail to be an abelian group under multiplication. Some special collections do pass, though: the 2 × 2 rotation matrices form an abelian group under matrix multiplication.

paragraphs.heading: A test with a table
paragraphs.text: For a finite group there is a quick check. Build its Cayley table, a grid set up the way a multiplication table is. The group is abelian exactly when the grid mirrors itself across its main diagonal, so that the entry in row i, column j equals the entry in row j, column i. That match is just the statement gᵢ⋅g_j = g_j⋅gᵢ.

paragraphs.heading: Abelian groups as ℤ-modules
paragraphs.text: Abelian groups lie underneath fields, rings, vector spaces and algebras; every ring, for instance, is an abelian group under its addition. Written additively, a whole number n times an element x means x added to itself n times, and (−n)x means −(nx). This lets the integers scale the elements, which makes every abelian group a module over ℤ in exactly one way. Going the other direction, every ℤ-module is an abelian group under its addition, so the two ideas agree.

paragraphs.heading: Well understood
paragraphs.text: Abelian groups are generally easier to handle in theory than non-abelian ones, and the finite abelian groups are completely classified. A finitely generated abelian group splits into two pieces. One is built from finitely many groups ℤ/p^kℤ, with p prime, joined in a direct sum, and the other is finitely many copies of ℤ, again joined in a direct sum. Among finite abelian groups, the simple ones are just the cyclic groups whose order is a prime.
